subsection: 3. Groups of hydrocarbons and their properties

notes.b: A hydrocarbon is a compound containing only carbon and hydrogen. Chemists sort hydrocarbons into groups by the kind of carbon–carbon bonds they contain, because the bonding decides how each group behaves.
points: Hydrocarbons are divided by the type of carbon–carbon bonds present into aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons.
Aliphatic hydrocarbons have open chains of carbon atoms, straight or branched, or rings that behave like chains, such as cyclohexane. They are the alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.
Aromatic hydrocarbons contain a benzene ring (a ring of six carbon atoms with special bonding). Benzene, C₆H₆, is the example given in the specification.
A saturated hydrocarbon (one holding as many hydrogens as it can) has only carbon–carbon single bonds, as in alkanes and cycloalkanes (alkanes whose carbons form a ring).
An unsaturated hydrocarbon contains at least one carbon–carbon double or triple bond, as in alkenes and alkynes, so it could take on more atoms by opening that bond.

A homologous series is a family with the same general formula (one formula that fits every member) and similar chemical properties, a gradual change in physical properties, and each member differing from the next by CH₂.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to define hydrocarbon, saturated, unsaturated, homologous series, aliphatic and aromatic, and to identify the series of a given compound. Aromatic means containing a benzene ring, not having a smell, and methane is aliphatic because it has no benzene ring.

notes.b: The alkanes are saturated aliphatic hydrocarbons with single bonds only. Having no multiple bonds explains why they are so unreactive.
points: General formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, where n is the number of carbons. The first members are methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀, pentane C₅H₁₂ and hexane C₆H₁₄.
Bonding: only single C–C and C–H covalent bonds are present, so the molecule is saturated.
Structure: each carbon is tetrahedral (its four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron), with bond angles of 109.5°. Chains can be branched from butane onwards.
Cyclohexane, C₆H₁₂, is a ring of six CH₂ groups joined by single bonds; it is saturated and aliphatic.
Cyclohexane has two fewer hydrogens than hexane because the ends of the chain are joined to make the ring. Its ring is not flat because each carbon is tetrahedral.
Alkanes are non-polar (their bonds have no significant positive or negative ends) and insoluble in water, and small members burn with a clean blue flame.
Alkanes are otherwise unreactive: they react with halogens (such as chlorine) only in ultraviolet light, by substitution (one atom replaced by another), e.g. CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.
notes.tip: Cyclohexane has the same formula (C₆H₁₂) as hexene but is saturated, so don't call it unsaturated. Reaction conditions and mechanisms are not required here.

notes.b: The alkenes are unsaturated aliphatic hydrocarbons with one carbon–carbon double bond. That double bond makes them far more reactive than alkanes.
points: General formula CₙH₂ₙ; the members are ethene C₂H₄, propene C₃H₆, butene C₄H₈, pentene C₅H₁₀ and hexene C₆H₁₂.
Bonding: one C=C double bond is present, so the molecule is unsaturated.
Structure: the two carbons of the double bond and the four atoms attached to them lie in one plane, with angles of about 120°, and there is no rotation about the C=C bond.
Alkenes are, like alkanes, non-polar and insoluble in water, but they are much more reactive.

Alkenes undergo addition (other atoms join on across the double bond, which becomes a single bond) with bromine, which decolourises bromine water (turns it from orange to colourless); with hydrogen over a nickel catalyst, e.g. CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃; and with hydrogen chloride, e.g. CH₂=CH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂Cl.

Alkenes add to one another to form addition polymers (long chains built from many alkene molecules), e.g. ethene forms poly(ethene). There is more on this in Types of organic reaction and addition polymers.
Alkenes burn with a more luminous (brighter), smokier flame than alkanes because of their higher carbon content.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to account for the greater reactivity of alkenes compared with alkanes, to draw the structure of ethene, and to identify the series of a given compound.

notes.b: The alkynes are unsaturated aliphatic hydrocarbons with one carbon–carbon triple bond. Like alkenes, they take part in addition reactions.
points: General formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂; the first member is ethyne, C₂H₂, also called acetylene.
Bonding: one C≡C triple bond is present, so the molecule is unsaturated.
Structure: the two carbons of the triple bond and the atoms attached to them lie in a straight line, with an angle of 180°, so ethyne is linear.
Alkynes undergo addition reactions; with excess bromine, ethyne gives 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane: C₂H₂ + 2Br₂ → CHBr₂CHBr₂.
Ethyne burns in air with a very smoky, luminous flame.
Ethyne burns in pure oxygen with a very hot flame, which is used for welding: 2C₂H₂(g) + 5O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to draw the structure of ethyne; remember it is linear, with a 180° angle.

notes.b: Benzene is the aromatic hydrocarbon on the course. It is unsaturated on paper, yet it behaves very differently from an alkene, and its structure explains why.
points: Benzene, C₆H₆, is a colourless liquid with a boiling point of 80 °C and a sweet smell.
Its structure is a flat, hexagonal ring of six carbon atoms, each bonded to one hydrogen atom, with bond angles of 120°.
All six carbon–carbon bonds are identical, intermediate in length between single and double bonds, because the electrons beyond the single bonds are delocalised (spread) around the whole ring.
This is why benzene is drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside. There is more on this in Shapes, bonding and isomerism.
Although benzene is unsaturated, it is very stable and resists addition: it does not decolourise bromine water or acidified potassium manganate(VII), and it reacts mainly by substitution.
Benzene burns with a very smoky, sooty flame because of its high carbon content, 92.3% by mass, the same as ethyne.
Benzene is toxic and carcinogenic (cancer-causing), causing leukaemia, so it is not used in school laboratories, where safer solvents such as cyclohexane are used instead.
Michael Faraday isolated benzene in 1825, and August Kekulé proposed a ring of alternating single and double bonds in 1865.
The Kekulé structure cannot explain why all the carbon–carbon bonds are the same length, or why benzene does not decolourise bromine water.
notes.tip: If asked whether benzene would readily undergo addition with bromine water, say no and explain: it is unsaturated but very stable because of its delocalised ring. Don't draw it with three fixed double bonds as if it were an alkene. Naming benzene derivatives (methylbenzene etc.) is not part of this subsection.

notes.b: Putting the four groups side by side shows a pattern: the type of carbon–carbon bonding decides the shape, the reactivity and the result of the bromine water test.
points: Alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, single C–C bonds, tetrahedral shape with 109.5° angles around each carbon, and methane as the first member; bromine water shows no change.
Alkenes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, one double bond, planar (flat) shape with 120° angles, and ethene as the first member; bromine water is decolourised.
Alkynes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, one triple bond, a linear shape with 180° angles, and ethyne as the first member; bromine water is decolourised.
Benzene has the general formula C₆H₆, a delocalised ring, a planar shape with 120° angles, and benzene as the first member; bromine water shows no change.

All four groups are non-polar, with only London dispersion forces (weak attractions between temporary charges in neighbouring molecules) between their molecules, so all are insoluble in water and soluble in non-polar solvents; small members are gases.

Reactivity follows bonding: single bonds only give unreactive alkanes; a localised double or triple bond gives reactive alkenes and alkynes that undergo addition; a delocalised ring gives benzene, which is stable and undergoes substitution rather than addition.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to compare alkanes, alkenes and alkynes by general formula, type of carbon–carbon bond and reaction with bromine water; a table with group, general formula, bond type, shape, first member and bromine water result covers it. Exams also ask you to account for the greater reactivity of alkenes compared with alkanes.

notes.h: IUPAC naming up to C6: stems and alkane rules
notes.b: Names follow the systematic IUPAC rules (the internationally agreed system), and only compounds up to C6 need to be named. Start with the stem and then work through the rules for alkanes.
points: The stem gives the number of carbons in the parent chain (the main chain): 1 meth-, 2 eth-, 3 prop-, 4 but-, 5 pent-, 6 hex-.
The ending is -ane for alkanes, -ene for alkenes and -yne for alkynes.
Find the longest continuous carbon chain, which may bend on paper; this gives the parent name.
Number the chain from the end that gives the side chains (substituents, groups branching off the main chain) the lowest numbers.
Name side chains as alkyl groups: methyl (–CH₃) and ethyl (–C₂H₅); give each a position number, using di- and tri- for repeats.
Separate numbers from one another with commas, and separate numbers from words with hyphens; list different side chains alphabetically.
notes.tip: Naming is required up to C6 only; don't name heptane or larger compounds. Exams ask you to give names from structures and to draw structures from names.

notes.b: Applying the rules to branched alkanes shows how the numbering works.
points: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃ is methylpropane. It needs no number because the methyl group can only be on carbon 2, though 2-methylpropane is also accepted.
CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is 2-methylbutane, not 3-methylbutane, because numbering from the end that gives the lowest number to the side chain puts it on carbon 2.
C(CH₃)₄ is 2,2-dimethylpropane, with di- showing two methyl groups, both on carbon 2.
CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is 3-methylpentane.
(CH₃)₂CHCH(CH₃)₂ is 2,3-dimethylbutane.

notes.h: IUPAC naming: alkenes, alkynes and rings
notes.b: Alkenes and alkynes follow the same rules, with one addition: the multiple bond decides the numbering and must sit in the main chain.
points: For alkenes and alkynes the main chain must contain the multiple bond; number from the end nearer to it, and give the number of its first carbon before -ene or -yne.
CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ is but-1-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃ is but-2-ene, CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₃ is 2-methylpropene, and CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ is hex-1-ene.
HC≡CCH₃ is propyne, and CH₃C≡CCH₃ is but-2-yne.
Ethene, propene, ethyne and propyne need no number, because there is only one position for the multiple bond.
Rings take the prefix cyclo-, as in cyclohexane; benzene keeps its own name.
notes.tip: Naming is required up to C6 only. You may be asked to draw a structure from a name, so practise going in both directions.

notes.b: Three things explain almost every difference in the properties of hydrocarbons: the forces between molecules, the size of the molecules, and the kind of carbon–carbon bond.
points: Hydrocarbons are non-polar, because C–H bonds have very low polarity (the electrons are shared almost equally), so the only forces between their molecules are London dispersion forces. There is more on this in Bond type and intermolecular forces.

London dispersion forces get stronger as relative molecular mass (Mr, the mass of a molecule compared with the carbon-12 standard) increases, because there are more electrons and larger electron clouds, and as the area of contact between molecules increases.

The stronger the intermolecular forces, the more energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the higher the boiling point and the more likely the substance is a liquid or solid at room temperature.
The nature of the carbon–carbon bonds decides chemical reactivity: single bonds only give unreactive compounds, while a C=C double bond gives reactivity through addition reactions.
Boiling overcomes the forces between molecules; it does not break C–C or C–H bonds.
notes.tip: Reactivity is asked for aliphatics only, so don't compare benzene's reactivity here.

notes.h: Straight-chain alkanes: boiling point and state
notes.b: The data show how boiling point depends on carbon number in the straight-chain alkanes (those with no branches).
points: Boiling points: methane −162 °C, ethane −89 °C, propane −42 °C, butane −1 °C, pentane 36 °C and hexane 69 °C.
Boiling point rises with carbon number because each extra CH₂ increases the relative molecular mass and the number of electrons, and lengthens the molecule, so London dispersion forces get stronger.
The rise for each extra CH₂ gets smaller: the successive differences are 73, 47, 41, 37 and 33 °C, because each CH₂ is a smaller fraction of the molecule.
At room temperature, about 20 °C, methane to butane are gases, while pentane and hexane are liquids.
Larger alkanes up to about C16 are liquids, and beyond that they are waxy solids.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain why boiling points rise along the alkane series (e.g. propane −42 °C, butane −1 °C), and to pick out the gases at room temperature from a table. The rises get smaller each time, so don't predict a straight line.

notes.h: Straight-chain alkanes: solubility, combustion and reactivity
notes.b: Other properties either follow from the molecules being non-polar or change gradually with chain length. Reactivity does not change at all.
points: All alkanes are insoluble in water, because they are non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.
All alkanes dissolve in or mix with non-polar solvents such as cyclohexane, following the rule “like dissolves like”.
Liquid alkanes are less dense than water and float on it; hexane has a density of about 0.66 g cm⁻³.
All alkanes burn completely to CO₂ and H₂O, e.g. C₆H₁₄(l) + 9½O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 7H₂O(l); larger alkanes need more oxygen per mole and release more energy per mole.
Larger alkanes burn with a more luminous, smokier flame and are less volatile (they evaporate less easily), so they are harder to ignite.
The percentage of carbon rises from 75.0% in CH₄ to 83.7% in C₆H₁₄, making incomplete combustion (burning in too little oxygen, giving soot and CO) more likely.
There is no difference in reactivity: all straight-chain alkanes are unreactive, reacting only by combustion or by substitution with halogens in ultraviolet light.
notes.tip: The question says differences, if any: for reactivity within the series, the honest answer is no significant difference, so say so and explain why. Describe alkanes as insoluble in water and give the reason (non-polar, no hydrogen bonding with water).

notes.h: Isomers of the same carbon number: boiling points
notes.b: Alkanes with the same carbon number but different structures are structural isomers: they have the same molecular formula and Mr, but a different arrangement of the chain. Their boiling points differ even so.
points: Butane (−1 °C) and methylpropane (−12 °C) are the isomers of C₄H₁₀.
Pentane (36 °C), 2-methylbutane (28 °C) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (10 °C) are the isomers of C₅H₁₂.
Hexane (69 °C), 3-methylpentane (63 °C), 2-methylpentane (60 °C), 2,3-dimethylbutane (58 °C) and 2,2-dimethylbutane (50 °C) are the isomers of C₆H₁₄.
The more branched the molecule, the more compact, or closer to spherical, it is, so the area of contact between neighbouring molecules is smaller.
Smaller contact gives weaker London dispersion forces and a lower boiling point, since the Mr is the same for all the isomers. Unbranched chains lie alongside each other with a large area of contact.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain why branched isomers have lower boiling points than straight-chain isomers. Remember that the isomers have the same Mr; the difference is surface area (shape), not mass.

notes.h: Isomers of the same carbon number: state, chemistry and diagram
notes.b: Branching changes the boiling point enough to change the state at room temperature, but it leaves the chemistry unchanged.
points: 2,2-dimethylpropane, with a boiling point of 10 °C, is a gas at room temperature, although pentane, with the same formula, is a liquid at room temperature because its boiling point is 36 °C.

Isomers show no significant difference in solubility, combustion or reactivity: all are non-polar and insoluble in water, burn to the same products with the same equation, e.g. C₅H₁₂ + 8O₂ → 5CO₂ + 6H₂O, and are equally unreactive.
Diagram: two pentane molecules lying side by side with a large area of contact, beside two 2,2-dimethylpropane molecules touching at only a small area.
notes.tip: For solubility between isomers, the honest answer is no significant difference; say so and explain why.

notes.h: Straight-chain alkenes: boiling point and state
notes.b: The monounsaturated straight-chain alkenes (those with one double bond and no branches) show the same boiling point pattern as the alkanes, but a little lower.
points: Boiling points: ethene −104 °C, propene −48 °C, but-1-ene −6 °C, pent-1-ene 30 °C and hex-1-ene 63 °C.
Boiling point rises with carbon number for the same reason as in alkanes: a larger Mr, more electrons and stronger London dispersion forces.
Ethene to butene are gases at room temperature, while pentene and hexene are liquids.

Each alkene boils a little lower than the alkane with the same number of carbons, e.g. ethene −104 °C against ethane −89 °C and hex-1-ene 63 °C against hexane 69 °C, because it has two fewer hydrogen atoms, so slightly fewer electrons and weaker London forces.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain why alkene boiling points increase, why hex-1-ene boils lower than hexane, and to predict the state of a hydrocarbon from a table.

notes.h: Straight-chain alkenes: solubility, combustion and reactivity
notes.b: Alkenes resemble alkanes in solubility, but their double bond makes their reactivity and flame different.
points: All alkenes are insoluble in water and soluble in non-polar solvents, like alkanes.
All alkenes burn to CO₂ and H₂O, e.g. C₃H₆(g) + 4½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l).
Every straight-chain alkene has the same percentage of carbon, 85.7%, since all have the formula CₙH₂ₙ; this is more than in the alkanes, so alkenes burn with smokier flames than alkanes.
All alkenes have one C=C bond, so they all undergo the same addition reactions, e.g. all decolourise bromine water, and they are much more reactive than alkanes.
Changing the chain length or the position of the double bond makes little difference to reactivity.
notes.tip: Exams ask why ethene is insoluble in water but soluble in cyclohexane: it is non-polar, so it mixes with the non-polar solvent but not with water. Within a series, reactivity does not change, so answer no significant difference.

notes.b: Use the data tables to predict properties from the trends. Each prediction rests on the three factors: intermolecular forces, Mr and bonding.
points: To predict a boiling point, use the trend in a table: the value lies between those of the neighbouring members, or of isomers with more and less branching.
Pent-1-ene, with a boiling point of 30 °C, is a liquid at 20 °C but would boil on a warm day or in warm water.
2-Methylpentane boils below hexane, because both are C₆H₁₄ and the branched isomer has a smaller area of contact.
Hex-1-ene will decolourise bromine water and hexane will not, and both will float on water without dissolving.
A mixture of pentane and hexane can be separated by fractional distillation (separating liquids by their different boiling points), because their boiling points differ, at 36 °C and 69 °C.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to predict the boiling point or state of a hydrocarbon from a table of data. Give the reason with every prediction.

notes.b: Of the aliphatic hydrocarbons, alkanes are the most stable. Stable here has a particular meaning, set out below.
points: Alkanes are the least reactive aliphatic hydrocarbons: at room temperature they do not react with acids, bases, most oxidising agents such as acidified potassium manganate(VII), or bromine water.
Their old name, paraffins, comes from the Latin parum affinis, meaning little affinity, that is, little reactivity.
“Stable” means unreactive under ordinary conditions, not that alkanes can never react: they burn readily once ignited, and they react with halogens in ultraviolet light.
notes.tip: Alkanes are not inert: they burn and undergo substitution. Exams ask you to explain why alkanes are relatively unreactive.

notes.h: Reasons for stability: saturation and low polarity
notes.b: Three features of alkane bonding explain their stability: they are saturated, their bonds are strong, and their bonds are almost non-polar.
points: Alkanes are saturated: every carbon already has four single bonds, so nothing can add to the molecule, and a bond must be broken before any reaction can occur.
C–C and C–H bonds are strong, so a great deal of energy is needed to break them, which gives a high activation energy (the minimum energy needed to start a reaction).

The electronegativities (a measure of how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons) of carbon, 2.55, and hydrogen, 2.20, differ by only 0.35, so C–H bonds are almost non-polar, and C–C bonds are completely non-polar.
With no significant δ⁺ or δ⁻ sites (slightly positive or negative ends), alkane molecules do not attract ions such as OH⁻ or H⁺, or polar molecules, which react by attacking charged sites.
Alkenes are more reactive because the C=C double bond is an electron-rich site that attracts reagents such as bromine and allows addition.
notes.tip: Use the electronegativity values 2.55 and 2.20, not the older 2.5 and 2.1. Exams ask you to explain why alkanes are unreactive and to account for the greater reactivity of alkenes.

notes.b: Alkanes are stable, not inert. They react under two sets of conditions: when ignited, and when exposed to ultraviolet light with a halogen.
points: Combustion: alkanes burn in oxygen once a flame or spark supplies the activation energy, releasing a lot of energy, e.g. CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).

Substitution with chlorine or bromine needs ultraviolet light, or sunlight, to split the halogen molecule into reactive atoms, called free radicals, e.g. CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl. There is more on this in Reaction mechanisms.
In the dark, an alkane mixed with bromine stays orange; in sunlight the colour slowly fades as substitution happens, which is much slower than the instant decolourisation produced by an alkene.
notes.tip: If asked what conditions an alkane needs to react with chlorine, say ultraviolet light. Name substitution but don't describe the mechanism steps here.

notes.b: The unreactivity of alkanes is useful in everyday life, and it also causes an environmental problem.
points: Alkanes are safe to store and transport as fuels, such as natural gas, LPG and petrol, because they do not react until ignited.
Unreactive liquid alkanes such as hexane and cyclohexane are useful solvents.
Mineral oils and paraffin wax are used as lubricants and protective coatings.

The same chemical stability makes poly(ethene) and other addition polymers, whose chains are alkane-like, slow to break down in the environment. There is more on this in Types of organic reaction and addition polymers.

notes.h: Sigma bonding and stability (Higher Level only)
notes.b: At Higher Level the stability of alkanes is explained by the type of bond. Single bonds are sigma bonds, while the second bond in an alkene's double bond is a weaker pi bond.
points: Every bond in an alkane is a sigma (σ) bond, formed by head-on overlap of orbitals (the regions where electrons are found) along the line between the two nuclei.
In a σ bond the shared electron pair is concentrated between the two nuclei, where both nuclei hold it strongly, so σ bonds are strong and their electrons are not exposed to attacking reagents.

An alkene's double bond is one σ bond plus one pi (π) bond; the π electrons lie above and below the plane of the molecule, further from the nuclei and less tightly held, so they are exposed to attack by electron-seeking reagents.

Typical average bond enthalpies (energies needed to break a bond) are C–C 348 kJ mol⁻¹, C=C 614 kJ mol⁻¹ and C–H 412 kJ mol⁻¹, so the π part of the C=C bond adds only about 266 kJ mol⁻¹ to the σ bond.
So alkenes react by breaking the weaker π bond and keeping the σ bond, which is addition, whereas an alkane would have to break a strong σ bond, which needs much more energy.
Diagram: a C–C σ bond with electron density between the nuclei, beside a C=C bond showing the σ bond and the π electron cloud above and below the bond axis.
notes.tip: A π bond is weaker than a σ bond, but a double bond (σ + π) is stronger than a single bond, so don't say double bonds are weak. Exams ask you to explain, in terms of sigma and pi bonding, why ethene reacts with bromine but ethane does not.

keyTerms.definition: A hydrocarbon with open chains of carbon atoms, or rings that behave like chains, and no benzene ring.
A hydrocarbon containing a benzene ring.
Containing only carbon–carbon single bonds, so that no further atoms can be added to the molecule.
Containing at least one carbon–carbon double or triple bond.
A family of compounds with the same general formula, similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties, each member differing from the next by CH₂.
A group of carbon and hydrogen atoms derived from an alkane, such as methyl or ethyl, attached to the parent chain as a side chain.
The longest continuous carbon chain in a molecule, which gives the stem of its name.
The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, which sets the systematic naming rules for compounds.
A prefix showing that a hydrocarbon forms a ring of carbon atoms.
Weak intermolecular forces, caused by temporary dipoles, that act between all molecules and increase with relative molecular mass and area of contact.
The attractions between neighbouring molecules, which are overcome, not broken bonds, when a substance boils.
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in a molecule, written Mr.
The part of a molecule's surface that touches its neighbours, which is larger for straight-chain molecules than for branched isomers.
The principle that substances dissolve in solvents of similar polarity, so non-polar hydrocarbons dissolve in non-polar solvents.
Containing one carbon–carbon double bond.
Evaporating readily, which is the property of a substance with a low boiling point.
The ability of an atom to attract the bonding electrons in a covalent bond.
The minimum energy that particles must have for a reaction to begin.
A reactive atom with an unpaired electron, formed when ultraviolet light splits a halogen molecule.
A reaction in which one atom or group in a molecule is replaced by another.
The old name for the alkanes, from the Latin for little affinity.
A covalent bond formed by head-on overlap of orbitals along the line joining two nuclei.
A covalent bond formed by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the line joining two nuclei.
The energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in gaseous molecules.

questions.prompt: Compare alkanes, alkenes and alkynes in terms of general formula, the type of carbon–carbon bond, and their reaction with bromine water.
questions.model: Alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and contain only single carbon–carbon bonds, so they are saturated; they do not decolourise bromine water. Alkenes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ and contain one carbon–carbon double bond, so they are unsaturated; they decolourise bromine water by addition. Alkynes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ and contain one carbon–carbon triple bond, so they are unsaturated; they decolourise bromine water by addition.

questions.prompt: Give the IUPAC names of: (i) CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, (ii) CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃, (iii) (CH₃)₂CHCH(CH₃)₂. Draw the structure of 2,2-dimethylbutane.
questions.model: (i) 2-methylbutane: the longest chain has four carbons, giving the parent butane, with a methyl group on carbon 2. (ii) pent-2-ene: a five-carbon chain with the double bond starting at carbon 2. (iii) 2,3-dimethylbutane: a four-carbon chain with methyl groups on carbons 2 and 3. 2,2-dimethylbutane is CH₃C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₃: a four-carbon chain with two methyl groups on carbon 2, drawn with every carbon and its bonds shown.

questions.prompt: Benzene is unsaturated, yet it does not decolourise bromine water. Explain, and describe the structure of benzene.
questions.model: Benzene is a flat, hexagonal ring of six carbon atoms, each bonded to one hydrogen atom, with bond angles of 120°. All six carbon–carbon bonds are identical and intermediate in length between single and double bonds, because the electrons beyond the single bonds are delocalised around the whole ring. Kekulé's alternating-bond structure cannot explain the equal bond lengths. This delocalisation makes benzene very stable, so it resists addition, which would break up the ring; it reacts by substitution instead, and so does not decolourise bromine water.

questions.prompt: The boiling points of pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are 36 °C, 28 °C and 10 °C. All three have the formula C₅H₁₂. Explain the difference and state which is a gas at 20 °C.
questions.model: All three are structural isomers with the same Mr, so the difference comes from shape rather than mass. Pentane is unbranched, so its molecules lie alongside each other with a large area of contact; its London dispersion forces are the strongest, giving the highest boiling point of 36 °C. The more branched isomers are more compact, with a smaller area of contact, so their London dispersion forces are weaker and their boiling points are lower: 28 °C for 2-methylbutane and 10 °C for 2,2-dimethylpropane. At 20 °C, 2,2-dimethylpropane, with a boiling point of 10 °C, is a gas, while pentane and 2-methylbutane are liquids.

questions.prompt: Explain why the boiling points of the alkenes ethene to hex-1-ene increase, why hex-1-ene boils at a lower temperature than hexane, and whether you would expect any difference in their solubility in water.
questions.model: The boiling points rise from ethene, −104 °C, through propene, −48 °C, but-1-ene, −6 °C, and pent-1-ene, 30 °C, to hex-1-ene, 63 °C, because the relative molecular mass and the number of electrons increase, so London dispersion forces get stronger. Hex-1-ene boils at 63 °C, lower than hexane at 69 °C, because it has two fewer hydrogen atoms, so slightly fewer electrons and weaker London dispersion forces. There is no significant difference in solubility in water: all the alkenes are non-polar, cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, and are insoluble in it.

questions.prompt: Hexane and hex-1-ene are both colourless liquids. Predict and explain one way in which their chemical properties differ and one way in which their combustion differs.
questions.model: Chemical properties: hex-1-ene has a C=C double bond and undergoes addition reactions, so it decolourises bromine water; hexane has only single bonds, is unreactive, and does not decolourise bromine water. Combustion: both burn completely to CO₂ and H₂O, but hex-1-ene, with 85.7% carbon by mass, burns with a smokier flame than hexane, which has 83.7% carbon.

questions.prompt: Explain the relative chemical stability of the alkanes, using electronegativity values (C 2.55, H 2.20).
questions.model: Alkanes are saturated, with four single bonds around each carbon, so no atoms can add to them and a bond must be broken before a reaction can occur. The C–C and C–H bonds are strong, so a high activation energy is needed to break them. The electronegativities of C, 2.55, and H, 2.20, differ by only 0.35, so C–H bonds are almost non-polar and C–C bonds are completely non-polar. Alkanes therefore have no δ⁺ or δ⁻ sites to attract ions or polar reagents, so they resist attack.

questions.prompt: Explain, in terms of sigma and pi bonding, why ethene reacts rapidly with bromine but ethane does not.
questions.model: Ethane has only σ bonds, with no π bonds. Its σ bonds are strong, and their electrons are held between the two nuclei, so they are not exposed to bromine. Ethene has a C=C double bond made of one σ bond and one π bond. The π electrons lie above and below the plane of the molecule, further from the nuclei and less tightly held, so they are exposed to attack by bromine. The π bond is weaker than a σ bond, adding only about 266 kJ mol⁻¹ to it, so it is the bond that breaks, and bromine adds across the double bond while the σ bond is kept, which is why ethene reacts rapidly.

questions.prompt: Alkanes are described as stable, yet methane burns explosively. Explain, and give one other reaction of alkanes with its condition.
questions.model: Alkanes are stable under ordinary conditions because they are unreactive at room temperature, but once ignited methane burns in oxygen, releasing a lot of energy: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). The flame or spark supplies the activation energy needed to start the reaction. Another reaction is substitution with chlorine, which needs ultraviolet light or sunlight to split the Cl₂ molecule into reactive atoms: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.
